newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget cuts make regional sales data scarce.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget cuts make regional sales data scarce.

text.p: Getting data on spending patterns between the East Coast, West Coast and most everywhere in between just got a whole lot harder.

Due to further budget cuts, the Commerce Department released its final regional retail sales report (for December) on February 27, albeit with little fanfare. The department is expected to save $1 million a year.
Economists said that even though the report virtually went unnoticed by U.S. financial markets, its absence will eventualy be felt.
Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said the data were useful in figuring out the differences in retail sales among various regions.

"The West Coast could be different from the central and eastern parts of the country," said Niemira, known for tracking sales information. And, "there are differences not only between regions, but within neighboring states in the same region."
Indeed, Niemira pointed out that in 1996, total sales in the mountain states "boomed," follwed by those in New England. But Central states did not fare as well.

According to Commerce, the now defunct report -- issued on a one-month lag compared to the widely-watched national sales report -- broke down retail sales data into four regions, nine sub-regions, 19 states and 44 large cities and areas.
The data were also broken down into categories, such as autos, general merchandise, apparel and furniture -- known as GAF -- and everything else.
Nancy Piesto, chief of the Commerce's monthly retail sales branch, said the data for both the regional and national surveys were collected together.
Whereas Commerce used to poll 11,000 retailers a month for their total national sales and sales figures for each store, only the total will now be asked, Piesto said.

Until recently, the regional data were partly funded an undisclosed amount by the New York-based International Council of Shopping Centers. But a spokeswoman for the group said they stopped funding because they "didn't see value in it as compared to what it was costing."
Niemira lamented the loss of the report, even though the "market never looked at it."
"There's a lot of data Commerce collected that no one ever heard of," he said. "It's just bad marketing. Because it was never promoted, no one knew it existed."
But Niemira said he plans to compile and put out regional sales data, although it likely will not be as detailed as the Commerce's report.
"It will be an estimate," he said. Niemira said he will gather regional data from TeleCheck, consumer confidence reports and other anecdotal reports.
"A lot of regional data are viewed as not terribly important from a national policy standpoint," he said. "But it is quite important from a regional policy standpoint."
